missingCandidates.title: Why Does Bromine Sometimes Add to an Alkene and at Other Times Abstract an Allylic Hydrogen Atom? A Computational Investigation of Hydrogen Bromide Addition and Allylic Bromination
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract The mechanisms of radical-mediated addition of hydrogen bromide to an alkene and of allylic bromination rely on a balance between competing addition and hydrogen abstraction by the bromine radical. In the past, addition has been postulated to be rapid and reversible, while abstraction is much slower but thermodynamically more favorable. G4 calculations are used to investigate this scenario in the case of cyclohexene. While generally supportive of the standard interpretation of the reaction, the calculations suggest that the kinetic barrier to hydrogen abstraction is often more entropic than enthalpic. A variety of other alkenes are also studied to test the limits of this framework. While the barriers to abstraction and the stability of the abstraction and addition radicals vary widely, only in the most extreme cases, such as cyclobutene, cyclopropene, and α-methylstyrene, do these variations compromise the balance between the competing reactions to an extent that interferes with effective allylic bromination. It was also observed that some bromine addition radicals are bridged in structure, especially the more highly substituted ones, while chlorine addition radicals are only rarely bridged.

missingCandidates.title: Aberrant one-carbon metabolism and ancestral genetics underlie edematous severe acute malnutrition
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Edematous severe childhood malnutrition is distinct from the non-edematous form of malnutrition and remains a major cause of under-five mortality. Its etiology remains unclear, although aberrant one-carbon metabolism has emerged as a potential contributor. Here, we assess genetic variants at loci known to influence one-carbon metabolism, and determine their association with edematous malnutrition in Jamaica and Malawi. Six loci show evidence of association, including four related to homocysteine and folate metabolism - AHCYL1 , PRICKLE2 , GABBR2 , and PLD2 , with SNPs at the latter three also having direct effects on homocysteine-related metabolites in Mendelian Randomization. Collectively, one-carbon metabolism-related variants were significantly associated with edematous malnutrition (z = 3.2), with population differences linked to a shared East African genetic ancestry and distinct signatures of selection. These findings strengthen evidence implicating aberrant one-carbon metabolism in edematous malnutrition and highlight the utility of cell-free DNA, intra-continental admixture, and population genetics for mapping disease risk.

missingCandidates.title: Computationally Guided Design of Facet-Defined Multielement Active Sites on Hexagonal Close-Packed High-Entropy-Alloy Nanosheets for Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Nonconventional hexagonal close-packed (HCP) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) provide distinct catalytic surfaces, but their synthesis with well-defined facets remains challenging, leaving facet-dependent multielement ensemble effects largely unexplored. Here, we report the computationally guided realization of atomically thin RuRhIrPtPd HEA nanosheets with predominantly exposed HCP {001} facets for the alkaline hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Density functional theory (DFT) calculations identify HCP {001} as the most favorable facet over {100} and {110}, where near-thermoneutral hydrogen adsorption, narrow energy distribution, and balanced hydrogen/hydroxyl binding create an optimized alkaline HER landscape. Guided by this prediction, RuRhIrPtPd HEA atomic layers are epitaxially grown on HCP Ru nanosheets to maximize {001} exposure, with atomic-resolution electron microscopy and synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) confirming atomically mixed HEA layers. Electrochemical measurements demonstrate that the {001}-faceted HEA nanosheets exhibit higher alkaline HER activity and durability than irregular-faceted nanocrystal counterparts and commercial Pt/C. Climbing-image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) calculations, operando XAS, and CO-stripping measurements identify Ru-centered ensembles as favorable Volmer sites, showing the lowest water-dissociation barrier of 1.04 eV compared with 1.13–1.47 eV for other metal sites, while neighboring multimetallic sites balance hydrogen and hydroxyl adsorption. This work provides a structural blueprint for harnessing facet-defined multielement ensembles to design high-entropy electrocatalysts.

missingCandidates.title: Coordination-Controlled Stability of Pd Single-Atom Catalysts under Electrochemical Conditions
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Single-atom catalysts (SACs) maximize atom utilization and site-specificity for diverse chemical and electrochemical transformations. While activity and selectivity have been optimized through advanced synthetic methods, the electrochemical stability of SACs remains insufficiently understood and limits practical application. Here, we employ operando inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) to quantify the dissolution kinetics of palladium (Pd) SACs in acidic electrolyte across a wide potential window. Operando electrochemically coupled mass spectrometry (EC-MS) confirms concurrent carbon support corrosion. By systematically varying heteroatom dopants, applied potentials, electrolyte pH, and adsorbing anions, we decouple coordination-driven (intrinsic) and electrochemical (extrinsic) factors controlling metal leaching. Specifically, the external potential exhibits a more pronounced influence on the stability of Pd SACs, while the coordinating heteroatoms modulate stability through both direct interaction with the isolated Pd centers and influence on the carbon support. Complementary X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) reveal dynamic restructuring of the Pd coordination environment, linking local chemical structure to macroscopic stability. These results provide mechanistic insights into SAC degradation pathways and establish design principles for stable single-atom architectures in energy conversion applications.

missingCandidates.title: Deep-Red Photocatalysis via Charge-Transfer Excitation of a Dicationic Ru(II) Sensitizer Using 740 nm Light
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract We report rare examples of deep-red Ru(II) photochemistry from a charge-transfer (CT) excited state using [Ru(bpy)2(p-biphe)](PF6)2 (bpy = 2,2′-bipyridine; p-biphe = 6,6′,7,7′-biphenanthridine). The absorption of deep-red light (740 nm) generates a dark but reactive CT excited state that can be harnessed in proof-of-principle reductive and oxidative electron-transfer and energy-transfer photocatalysis.

missingCandidates.title: Insertion of Alkenes into Aryl Nitrile C–C Bonds Enabled by Thiophenolate Photocatalysis
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Insertion of alkenes into chemical bonds represents a powerful strategy for carbon framework editing, yet direct insertion into C–C bonds remains a formidable challenge due to the nonpolarity, high-lying σ* orbital, steric shielding, and high thermodynamic stability of the C–C bond. Here, we present a visible-light-driven thiophenolate photocatalytic system that enables direct insertion of alkenes into the C–C bond of aryl nitriles. Mechanistic studies reveal a photoinduced single-electron transfer from the excited thiophenolate anion to the aryl nitrile, generating a radical pair that undergoes radical addition and radical–radical cross-coupling, followed by elimination and nucleophilic addition to afford the insertion product. This strategy not only provides an avenue for editing inert C–C bonds but also establishes thiophenolate photocatalysis as a platform for challenging bond constructions under transition-metal-free and redox-neutral conditions.

missingCandidates.title: Photoenzymatic Enantioselective [2+2] Cycloaddition of Alkynes Enabled by Whole-Cell Directed Evolution
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Enantioselective excited-state photocycloadditions represent an attractive yet challenging strategy for accessing optically active strained molecules. Here, we report a whole-cell directed evolution platform for engineering artificial triplet photoenzymes that catalyze the enantioselective [2 + 2] photocycloaddition of alkynes. By employing calcium chloride-mediated membrane permeabilization, we overcome substrate accessibility limitations in whole-cell systems and enable high-throughput evolution without the need for cell lysates or purified enzymes. Through ten rounds of directed evolution, a primitive ancestor (APC1.0; 46% yield, 6% ee) was transformed into a highly efficient variant (APC10.0; 92% yield, 94% ee under whole-cell conditions; 99% yield, 97% ee as the purified enzyme). The enhanced activity of APC10.0 enabled a total turnover number of 1800. This work establishes a generalizable strategy for the evolution of artificial photoenzymes and expands the scope of biocatalysis toward stereoselective excited-state transformations.

missingCandidates.title: Quantified Structure–Performance Relationships for Fe(III)K(I) Heterodinuclear Catalysts in Cyclohexene Oxide/CO2 Ring-Opening Copolymerization
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Catalyst design and understanding are improved by quantified structure–performance relationships, but these are underutilized in polymerization catalysis. In epoxide/carbon dioxide ring-opening copolymerization (ROCOP), an important route to make polymers from bio- and waste-based feedstocks, significant success has been achieved in understanding cobalt catalysts, but understanding of other metal catalysts is much less developed. This work targets earth-abundant bimetallic catalysts featuring iron and potassium. A series of seven Fe(III)K(I) catalysts, coordinated by different ancillary ligands, are compared with analogues Co(III)K(I) catalysts; the iron catalysts demonstrate both high activity (TOF = 675 h–1) and polymer selectivity (98%) in cyclohexene oxide/carbon dioxide copolymerization (20 bar CO2 pressure, 100 °C). The Fe(III)K(I) catalysts also show a linear free energy relationship between the copolymerization rates and the catalyst ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) wavelength, with a volcano relationship identifying the best catalysts. The most active catalysts have an Fe(III) center with an intermediate LMCT wavelength, and these features are consistent with the proposed copolymerization mechanism. In this field of catalysis, quantified structure-performance relationships are very rare; thus, the findings are fundamentally interesting and should help to accelerate the design of better-performing iron-based polymerization catalysts.

missingCandidates.title: Spatial Separation of Metal–MOF Tuning Catalytic Selectivity in CO2 Hydrogenation and Methanol Partial Oxidation
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Tuning the interactions between metal nanoparticles (NPs) and metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) is pivotal for selective catalysis, yet systematic regulation of metal–MOF spatial separation remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that systematically regulating the metal–MOF separation enables controlled modulation of catalytic activity and reaction selectivity. A series of MOF-encapsulated Pt catalysts with adjusted Pt–MOF separations were designed and synthesized by varying the surface coverage of capping agents on Pt NPs. Both CO2 hydrogenation and methanol partial oxidation exhibit volcano-type dependencies of catalytic performance on Pt–MOF separation, revealing the existence of an optimal spatial window for catalytic cooperation between Pt NPs and MOF nodes. Theoretical calculations indicate that an appropriate Pt–MOF separation facilitates the formation of key reaction intermediates, thereby governing catalytic selectivity. This work establishes metal–MOF spatial separation as an important structural parameter for catalyst design and provides a practical strategy for developing proximity-engineered NP–MOF catalysts with tunable reaction selectivity.

missingCandidates.title: Structural and Mechanistic Insight into Oxidative Ring Opening Catalyzed by L-DOPA Extradiol Dioxygenase from Beta vulgaris
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Betalain pigments replace anthocyanins in the majority of plants from the order Caryophyllales, but they are also present in some fungi and bacteria. Their biosynthesis attracts considerable scientific interest due to their applications across various fields and also because plant pigmentation is used to study complex evolution within Caryophyllales. The key step in betalain biosynthesis is the oxidative ring opening of L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (L-DOPA) catalyzed by L-DOPA extradiol dioxygenase (DODA, EC: 1.13.11.29), which yields 4,5-seco-DOPA; the latter cyclizes to betalamic acid, the chromophore of all betalains. Betalain-producing plants feature two to six homologues of DODA, yet only one of them is highly active and participates in the betalain biosynthesis. Here, we report the crystal structures of the highly active DODAα1 from Beta vulgaris (beetroot), the main commercial source of betalain pigments. High-resolution structures of the apo form and complexes with L-DOPA and three substrate analogues (4-nitrocatechol, 6-nitro-L-DOPA, mimosine) provide insights into the key interactions responsible for effective substrate recognition by the enzyme. Enzymatic reaction kinetics for WT BvDODAα1 show that the enzyme is three orders of magnitude more efficient than the previously studied homologue BvDODAα2, with a pH optimum of 6.5, and that the kinetics are affected by modest substrate inhibition. The residues selected based on X-ray structures for site-directed mutagenesis, except Asp81, are critical for efficient catalysis, whereas molecular dynamics simulations show that they form strong direct and through-water contacts with the L-DOPA amino acid side chain. Mössbauer spectroscopy, supported by DFT calculations, suggests that the catechol ring of L-DOPA

missingCandidates.title: Titanium-Catalyzed Divergent Deoxycyclization for Synthesizing Semisaturated Nitrogen Heterocycles
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Semisaturated nitrogen heterocycles, such as 3-pyrrolines and unsaturated azepanes, possess highly prized three-dimensional geometries for drug discovery. However, their divergent synthesis from simple, unactivated feedstocks remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report a highly selective, titanium-catalyzed divergent radical deoxycyclization coupling of nitrosoarenes and 1,3-dienes. Following an initial aza-Diels–Alder cycloaddition, an in situ generated low-valent titanium(III) species mediates single-electron homolytic cleavage of the robust oxazine N–O bond, yielding a transient nitrogen-centered aminyl radical. By rationally tuning the solvent coordination sphere and chlorosilane dissociation kinetics, this radical’s trajectory is selectively directed down two orthogonal pathways: a 5-exo-tet cyclization to afford 3-pyrrolines (formal [4 + 1]) and a highly strained vinylaziridine-mediated aza-Claisen rearrangement to yield unsaturated azepanes (formal [4 + 3]). This radical-polar crossover protocol features broad functional group tolerance and enables a streamlined, cyanide-free synthesis of the antiarrhythmic drug candidate SU-13197. Comprehensive mechanistic studies, including EPR spin-trapping, support the crucial aminyl radical intermediacy and the important role of titanium coordination in orchestrating cascade divergence.

missingCandidates.title: Understanding the Role of Band Bending and Surface Coordination in Steering Piezocatalytic In Situ H2O2 Evolution Routes
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Piezocatalytic H2O2 production, employing water and oxygen as the raw materials, is emerging as a promising and viable alternative for in situ H2O2 evolution. However, the understanding of the structure–activity relationship of piezocatalysts still poses challenges, and the key factor steering the H2O2 evolution pathway also remains ambiguous. Herein, two bismuth ferrite-based materials with different crystal structures, perovskite-type BiFeO3 and mullite-type Bi2Fe4O9, were prepared for a systematic comparison of their piezocatalytic activity and an in-depth investigation into the routes of H2O2 in situ production. As a result, BiFeO3 achieved a higher H2O2 production rate (252.86 μmol·L–1) than Bi2Fe4O9 (140.32 μmol·L–1) over 60 min in ambient aqueous conditions without any sacrificial agent. Mechanism analysis reveals that a higher piezocatalytic H2O2 yield of BiFeO3 arises from its stronger piezoelectric response and surface coordination mode of bridging hydroxyl groups. The piezoelectric-induced band bending made water oxidation thermodynamically feasible, and the bridging hydroxyl groups offered hole-transfer channels, thereby collectively triggering the simultaneous occurrence of oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) and water oxidation reaction (WOR). This work provides fundamental insights into the crystal-structure-dependent piezocatalytic activity, offering a profound understanding of the mechanism underlying H2O2 evolution routes.

missingCandidates.title: Untangling the Molecular Mechanism of SpCas9 HNH Domain Checkpoint Activation: A Gear-and-Wedge Fitting Model
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract The CRISPR-associated endonuclease Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpCas9) facilitates site-specific DNA cleavage, with structural transition from the checkpoint state to the catalytic conformation representing a critical activation step. This transition involves an approximately 38 Å displacement of the HNH domain catalytic residue H840 toward the target DNA. However, the molecular determinants governing this large-scale rearrangement of the HNH domain during checkpoint activation, and the conformational routes by which HNH repositioning may occur, remain incompletely understood. To address this knowledge gap, we combined nudged elastic band-guided sampling with unbiased molecular dynamics simulations, reaching a cumulative timescale of 160 μs, and constructed a kinetic model describing HNH domain dynamics during checkpoint activation with Markov state modeling. The mechanistic features suggested by these simulations were further evaluated through biochemical DNA cleavage assays and an intracellular fluorescence reporter system. Our results identify conformational plasticity of the L2 linker and coupled motion of the REC2 domain as key regulatory elements of the HNH domain relocation during SpCas9 checkpoint activation. The model suggests that L2 linker remodels toward a disassembled state to enable release and repositioning of the HNH domain, while the REC2 domain outward displacement guides HNH domain relocation through transient interactions that stabilize activation-associated intermediates. Site-directed mutagenesis of key residues in the L2 linker and REC2 domain significantly reduced DNA cleavage efficiency in both biochemical and cellular assays, supporting their functional importance in SpCas9 activation. Taken together, this study provides an experiment

missingCandidates.title: Cation‐Mediated Interface Engineering Directs Electrogenerated Reactive Oxygen Species Pathways
missingCandidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Persistent organic contaminants are increasingly accumulating in saline waters, where high ionic strength and complex electrolytes hinder oxidative remediation. Electrogenerated reactive oxygen species (ROS) offer a promising route for pollutant degradation, yet the role of electrolyte cations in controlling ROS pathways remains poorly understood. Although singlet oxygen ( 1 O 2 ) is more persistent and matrix‐tolerant than hydroxyl radicals (•OH), whether cation‐induced changes in interfacial water structure govern ROS selectivity remains unclear. Here, using atomically dispersed Cu on Fe 2 O 3 ‐carbon nanotubes (Cu 1 /Fe 2 O 3 ‐CNTs) as a dual‐ROS electrocatalyst, we show that alkali‐metal cations exert distinct effects on ROS generation. •OH production follows the expected cation‐size‐dependent trend, whereas 1 O 2 generation exhibits an anomalous maximum in Na + ‐containing electrolytes, leading to superior contaminant degradation. Quantitative ROS measurements, in situ electrochemical analysis, spectroscopy, and theoretical calculations show that this behavior is primarily governed by selective stabilization of the *OOH intermediate rather than enhanced O 2 adsorption. Na + promotes a highly interconnected interfacial hydrogen‐bond network that stabilizes *OOH and favors 1 O 2 formation. In natural seawater, this regulation enables 98.2% contaminant removal within 8 h at an estimated energy demand of 0.779 kWh m −3 . These findings identify electrolyte cations as important regulators of ROS selectivity and provide a basis for efficient saline‐water decontamination.

missingCandidates.title: Dibenzophenazine‐Fused Heterocyclic Luminophores: Decoding High‐Performance Organic Light‐Emitting Diodes Based on Long‐Wavelength Exciplex
missingCandidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Developing highly efficient long‐wavelength exciplexes remains a challenge due to the constraints of the energy gap law and severe non‐radiative loss. In this study, we report a rigid nitrogen‐rich donor, 3N, featuring the first fused framework constructed from two anti‐aromatic phenazine units. This unique architecture ensures 3N has good planarity and an exceptionally shallow highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level of −4.88 eV. Meanwhile, the effective suppression of structural relaxation by its rigid scaffold contributes to a narrow emission at 456 nm. By pairing 3N with planar boron‐containing acceptors through strong intermolecular interactions, highly efficient exciplex emissions ranging from green to orange‐red were successfully achieved. Two representative exciplex systems reached outstanding photoluminescence quantum yields of 92% at 557 nm and 78% at 604 nm, respectively. Correspondingly, organic light‐emitting diodes based on these exciplexes delivered maximum external quantum efficiencies of 25.6% at 556 nm and 24.7% at 586 nm, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, these values rank among the highest performance metrics reported for long‐wavelength exciplexes. These results demonstrate that fusing multiple phenazine units could significantly raise the HOMO level and enhances structural rigidity, thereby enabling highly efficient long‐wavelength exciplex electroluminescence.

missingCandidates.title: Linear and Branched Alkanes Separation Through Conjugated‐Polymer‐Framework Membranes
missingCandidates.abstract: ABSTRACT The separation of linear and branched alkanes is critically important for improving the research octane number (RON) and advancing the sustainable development of the petrochemical industry. However, owing to their nearly identical kinetic diameters and closely related physicochemical properties (e.g., solubility parameters and boiling points), membrane‐based liquid‐phase separation of such linear and branched alkanes remains highly challenging. An example is the n‐ heptane/ iso ‐octane pair, which exhibits minimal differences in molecular size and physicochemical properties but a dramatic difference in RON. Herein, we report a conjugated‐polymer‐framework (CPF) membrane that enables molecular‐level separation of linear and branched alkanes. The crystallized selective layer of CPF membrane features intrinsic sub‐nanometer pores of ∼5.5 and 8.4 Å. With ethanol as an assisting agent, the membrane achieves a separation factor of 5.24 for n ‐heptane/ iso ‐octane mixture, together with a total mixture permeance of 0.020 kg m −2 h −1 bar −1 . This pronounced selectivity stems from ethanol‐induced modulation of transmembrane transport, which selectively mitigates the transport barrier of linear alkanes while exerting negligible influence on their branched counterparts, thereby enhancing kinetic selectivity. Furthermore, the CPF membrane exhibits robust separation performance over extended operation and across a wide range of feed compositions and pressures, highlighting its robustness for linear/branched alkane separation.

missingCandidates.title: Asymmetric Elongation of Uranyl within a Silver Nanocluster
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Confinement within nanoscale cavities can profoundly alter molecular structure and electronic properties, but this strategy has never been applied to inherently linear and symmetric uranyl cations (UO22+). Here, we report the first example of uranyl encapsulation within a self-assembled silver nanocluster, [UO2F5@Ag21(CCBut)14](BF4)3F (CCBut = 3,3-dimethyl-1-butynyl), abbreviated as UO2F5@Ag21. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction reveals asymmetric elongation of the axial O ≡ U≡O bonds from the ideal symmetric value of 1.77 Å to 1.788(9) and 1.837(9) Å, respectively. Raman and IR spectroscopy show extreme redshifts of both symmetric and asymmetric stretching vibrations (ν1 down to 765 cm–1). Transient absorption spectroscopy further reveals an excited-state quenching process of the (UO2F5)3– guest driven by unique confinement. High-energy-resolved fluorescence detected X-ray absorption near edge structure (HERFD-XANES) at the U M4 edge demonstrates re-engineered 5f electronic states, with a shifted and broadened 5fσ* feature indicating reduced U≡O covalency. This work establishes nanoconfinement as a powerful new route to reshape the electronic structure and property of actinide-based materials.

missingCandidates.title: Catalytic Asymmetric 1,6-Diene Cyclization via Designed Carbocationic 5- and 6- exo Pathways
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Catalytic asymmetric electrophilic alkene functionalization provides a powerful strategy for the construction of complex chiral molecules. Despite significant progress in this field, the asymmetric functionalization of alkenes promoted by an electrophilic carbon species via an exo-cyclization mode remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report a solution to this challenge: alkenes can undergo designed 5-exo- and 6-exo-carbocationic cyclizations to generate optically pure, complex chiral compounds with high enantio- and diastereoselectivities. In this approach, for 1,6-dienes bearing bulky sulfonamide or quaternary carbon linkers, one double bond of the substrate interacts with an external electrophile, such as a trifluoromethylthio, arylthio, alkylthio, or chlorine species, generating an electrophilic carbon species that promotes the transformation of 1,6-dienes under chiral indane-based chalcogenide catalysis. Notably, the reaction can be terminated by intramolecular nucleophiles via cis-addition or can be captured by various intermolecular nucleophiles. A diverse array of optically pure polycyclic and monocyclic compounds can be obtained, including 5-5-6 tricyclic N-heterocycles and pentasubstituted chiral cyclohexanes. The same strategy can also be efficiently applied to 6-endo cyclizations, leading to the formation of 6-6-6 tricyclic and monocyclic N-heterocycles. The resulting products can be readily converted to various other valuable compounds, further demonstrating the utility of this methodology. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to rationalize the observed selectivities, revealing that the preferential transition-state conformations lower the activation barriers for the desired cyclization pathways. This work offers a vers

missingCandidates.title: Chemical Bonding Rules for Stacking-Sequence Stability in Bismuth Oxychloride Intergrowths and Their Consequences for Band Structure
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Metal oxyhalides are versatile materials, exhibiting properties relevant to photocatalysis, solid-state battery systems, ferromagnetism, multiferroics, and nonlinear optics. Here, mixed-metal oxyhalide intergrowths, layered materials formed by intercalating SrBi3O4Cl3 and Bi2GdO4Cl blocks along the c direction within a crystal, are reported. They are synthesized through a flux-based approach in which the SrBi3O4Cl3-to-Bi2GdO4Cl ratio can be precisely controlled. Despite the structural and compositional flexibility of such intergrowths, there is no general framework for predicting which local structural arrangements are preferred. Density functional theory combined with Bader charge analysis shows that preferred stacking sequences are those that minimize charge disproportionation across distinct chlorine environments, consistent with Pauling’s fifth rule, and we support this bonding-based framework through computational cation substitution that shifts the ionic-covalent balance of the metal–chloride bonding. With the preferred stacking arrangement established, this same system further reveals that intergrowth layering and Sr/Bi site occupancy modulate the interaction between the Bi3+ lone pair and anion p orbitals. Density functional theory calculations reveal that intergrowth formation destabilizes the O-2p orbitals, raising the valence band maximum for visible-light absorption, with the lone-pair interaction and layering-driven internal electrostatic field acting as competing effects on the resulting band gap. Significantly, this experimental-computational study establishes a transferable, bonding-based framework for stacking-sequence stability in layered oxyhalide intergrowths, while also clarifying how the same structural levers used to control stability can

missingCandidates.title: Clickable Photolabile Linkers for Convenient Immobilization and Light-Controlled Release of Substrates from Solid Support
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Photolabile linkers (PLLs) enable spatiotemporal control over substrate release but often suffer from slow photorelease kinetics, low quantum yields, or limited functionalization options. Here, we report a family of heterobifunctional PLLs based on (3-hydroxy-5-alkoxynaphthalen-2-yl)methyl (NQMP) chromophores that combine rapid, high-yielding photochemical cleavage with orthogonal conjugation chemistries for efficient substrate immobilization and light-triggered release. Six heterobifunctional NQMP-based linkers bearing terminal acetylene, cyclooctyne, amine, carboxyl, allyl, and biotin groups were synthesized and employed for the immobilization of fluorescent dyes, acetylsalicylic acid, biotin, avidin, and doxorubicin on silica microspheres and mesoporous silica nanoparticles. Mild UV-A irradiation resulted in efficient release of the attached payloads while preserving the integrity of the solid support. Mesoporous silica nanoparticles provide high loading capacity and are suitable for light-controlled drug delivery. The modular design, excellent photochemical efficiency, orthogonal conjugation chemistries, and compatibility with diverse substrates make NQMP-based PLLs versatile tools for reversible surface functionalization, controlled cargo release, affinity capture, and photoresponsive drug delivery applications.

missingCandidates.title: Direct Detection of the Calcium–Sodium–Calcium Metal Triad in Thermostable α-Amylases from Bacillus sp. Bacteria in Aqueous Solution by 23Na Quadrupole-Central-Transition NMR Spectroscopy
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract We report that the Na+ ion within the calcium–sodium–calcium (Ca–Na–Ca) metal triad in two thermostable bacterial α-amylases (ca. 58 kDa) can be directly detected by 23Na (I = 3/2) quadrupole-central-transition (QCT) NMR spectroscopy in aqueous solution. We show that 23Na QCT NMR signals from hyperthermostable Bacillus licheniformis α-amylase (BLA) and its mesophilic homologue, Bacillus amyloliquefaciens α-amylase (BAA), exhibit remarkable subppm spectral resolution, which is unprecedented in NMR studies of quadrupolar nuclei in proteins. Using this new 23Na QCT NMR methodology, we examine the pH-dependent unfolding, melting temperatures (Tm), long-term thermal inactivation profiles, and chemical denaturing of BAA and BLA. We also use 23Na QCT NMR to monitor EDTA titration experiments, which yielded the apparent binding constants of the Na+ ion to BAA and BLA to be (0.3 ± 0.1) × 109 and (0.6 ± 0.1) × 109 M–1, respectively. Because the Ca–Na–Ca metal triad is located in the vicinity of the active cleft, the subppm spectral resolution of 23Na QCT NMR makes it possible to detect subtle changes of the enzyme structure caused by the presence of inhibitors such as acarbose and quercetin. This work represents the first time that Na+ ions tightly bound to an enzyme are directly observed by 23Na QCT NMR in aqueous solution. This new 23Na QCT NMR approach can potentially be extended to detection of other metal ions with quadrupolar nuclei such as K+, Mg2+, and Zn2+ in metalloenzymes in their native aqueous environment.

missingCandidates.title: Giant Baromagnetic Effect Induced by Spin Engineering in Mn3(Zn0.25Sn0.25Ga0.25Ge0.25)C
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Baromagnetic effect (BME), arising from pressure-induced spin reorientation, holds great potential for next-generation information technologies owing to its strong multifield coupling characteristics. However, the practical implementation of BME is hindered by the small magnetization change and the large driving pressure required in conventional materials. Guided by spin-polarized calculations, this work successfully obtains a giant BME material Mn3(Zn0.25Sn0.25Ga0.25Ge0.25)C, which exhibits a remarkable pressure-induced maximum magnetization change (|ΔMmax|) of 2.63 μB·f.u.–1 and an exceptionally large baromagnetic coefficient (BMC, d) of 15.0 μB·f.u.–1·GPa–1. Temperature-dependent neutron powder diffraction (NPD) measurements reveal a clear evolution from the nearly collinear antiferromagnetic (cAFM) configuration with k = (1/2, 1/2, 1/2) to the ferromagnetic (FM) configuration, indicating that the spins are highly susceptible to reorientation under external perturbations. First-principles calculations further clarify that pressure modulates the energy difference (ΔE) between the cAFM and FM configurations via the Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) interaction, elucidating the microscopic origin of the giant BME. This demonstration establishes spin engineering, achieved through precise control of spin configurations via targeted element selection, as an effective strategy for realizing high-performance baromagnetic systems. It further provides clear guidance for designing materials with superior functional properties.

missingCandidates.title: Group Theory-Guided Orbital Symmetry Engineering of cis -Quinacridone: From Symmetry-Forbidden to Dipole-Allowed Transitions for Efficient Narrowband Emissions
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Although group theory is widely used to analyze symmetry and electronic transition selection rules in condensed matter physics and coordination chemistry, its use as a predictive design tool for organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) remains largely unexplored. This is particularly important for highly symmetric emitters, where orbital-symmetry constraints can render the lowest-energy transition symmetry-forbidden. Herein, guided by quantum-chemical and group-theoretical analyses, we revisit the long-known cis- and trans-quinacridone isomers and reveal that the lowest-energy transition of cis-quinacridone (cis-QA) is symmetry-forbidden, resulting in a negligible transition dipole moment and intrinsically weak emission. We address this limitation through a group theory-guided orbital-symmetry engineering strategy based on carbonyl-to-imine transformation of the cis-QA skeleton. This targeted structural modification reorganizes the frontier orbital symmetry, converting the lowest-energy transition from symmetry-forbidden to dipole-allowed, while preserving the rigid, highly symmetric molecular framework and suppressing excited-state structural relaxation and vibronic coupling. The resulting cis-I2A2 derivatives exhibit high photoluminescence quantum yields (ΦPL) of 70–99% and narrow emission bandwidths with full-widths at half-maximum (fwhm’s) of 20–32 nm. An OLED based on cis-I2A2-3 delivers narrowband yellow electroluminescence with an emission maximum at 550 nm, a maximum external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 32.4%, and substantially mitigated efficiency roll-off relative to conventional cis-quinacridone emitters. missingCandidates.title: Imaging of Electrochemically Programmed Single-Molecule Reactions
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Single-molecule reactions reveal intrinsic heterogeneity that is obscured in ensemble measurements. However, most existing approaches rely on extreme dilution, ultrasmall solution volumes, or physical confinement to keep individual events sufficiently sparse. Here, we introduce electrochemically programmed single-molecule reactions (PSMR), a pulse-regulated strategy that shifts single-molecule electrochemistry from passive observation to active control. It converts continuous interfacial reactions to a sequence of short, repeatable reaction trials. By tailoring the pulse waveform, PSMR controls the driving force and duration of each reaction trial, thereby regulating the probability of single-molecule reactions, while the relaxation interval between pulses allows the interface to recover before the next trial. This coordinated control enables single-molecule reactions to be actively regulated under conventional solution volumes and reaction concentrations. By coupling individual reaction events to single-photon emission through electrogenerated chemiluminescence (ECL), we can directly count and image the reactions. The ultrashort reaction windows and relaxation periods suppress diffusion-layer buildup, thereby preserving sensitivity to local reaction kinetics, even at high overpotentials. Using this approach, individual Au nanoparticles were imaged over a broad potential range, and particles as small as 5 nm were distinguished from the substrate background. Sparse photon events were accumulated over repeated trials and further analyzed using localization- and fluctuation-based algorithms, enabling super-resolution mapping of reaction activity beyond the optical diffraction limit. PSMR therefore provides a framework for actively regulating, quantitatively imagin

missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract We establish a kinetic strategy for controlling the supramolecular copolymerization of boron- and nitrogen-containing π-electron systems by exploiting intramolecular hydrogen bonding in cystine-based dimeric diamides. Two dimeric diamides bearing solubilizing alkyl chains, DBB and DNN, were designed and synthesized by functionalization with planarized triarylborane (PTAB) and planarized triarylamine (PTAA) units, respectively. In low-polarity solvents, both molecules form one-dimensional nanostructures upon ultrasonication. Intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the two diamide units within the cystine framework suppresses spontaneous nucleation and generates metastable monomeric states, thereby providing a kinetic window for seeded supramolecular polymerization. Despite a difference of more than 10 kJ mol–1 between their Gibbs free energy changes for homopolymerization, external cross-seeding with preformed DBB seeds initiates the supramolecular polymerization of metastable DNN monomers. The resulting supramolecular copolymers exhibit long-lived emission arising from spatially confined interactions between the PTAB and PTAA units. The extent of heteromolecular contact formation can be modulated by switching between external and internal cross-seeding protocols. In the internal cross-seeding process, DBB assemblies are generated in situ in the presence of DNN monomers, enabling their incorporation during supramolecular growth and producing coassemblies with an enhanced contribution of heteromolecular excited-state interactions. These results demonstrate that kinetic control over nucleation and elongation enables pathway-dependent regulation of heteromolecular contacts in equimolar binary supramolecular polymers with markedly different homopolymerization propen

missingCandidates.title: Multicomponent Nanocrystal Superlattice Structure Prediction from First-Principles Validated against Two Decades of Experiments
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Predicting nanocrystal (nanoparticle) assembly into ordered arrays (superlattices) is a grand challenge in materials chemistry that has largely resisted first-principles theories. Here, we extend MOLT-CF, a classical density functional theory, to multicomponent nanocrystal systems and subject it to a rigorous validation by comparing against nearly 300 experiments spanning two decades of literature. We use MOLT-CF to predict stability and phase diagrams for binary superlattices of nanocrystals with linear hydrocarbon ligands, as well as many other fine structural details, for example, lattice constants, packing fractions, ligand structure, and, in the case of (cubic) perovskite nanocrystals, orientation. Significant discrepancies from experiments are noted only for the Li3Bi and Cu3Au superlattices. In the former, we predict that this lattice is stabilized by particle fractionalization, which is supported by a reexamination of experimental data in the literature. In the case of Cu3Au (for which MOLT-CF predicts thermodynamic instability against phase separation into single-component lattices), we propose two alternative candidate structures that reconcile theory with experimental observations. These results establish MOLT-CF as a rigorous platform for the computational design of next-generation functional nanoparticle materials.

On-Surface Synthesis of a Low Bandgap Cyclopenta[ c , d ]azulene-Based Polymer
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Nonbenzenoid topologies offer a compelling strategy to tailor the electronic properties of low-dimensional carbon materials. Here, we report the on-surface synthesis of a nonalternant polymer incorporating a [7–5–5] cyclopenta[c,d]azulene (CPA) motif on Au(111) via thermally induced Ullmann coupling. Bond-resolved scanning tunneling microscopy confirms the robustness of the [7–5–5] framework. Scanning tunneling spectroscopy, together with dI/dV mapping supported by density functional theory calculations, reveals a remarkable narrow polymeric bandgap of 1.5 eV. The electronic structure is governed by the intramolecular charge transfer from the heptagonal ring to the adjacent fused pentagonal rings, resulting in a pronounced dipole moment despite being composed exclusively of carbon and hydrogen. Aromaticity analyses indicate the coexistence of locally aromatic and slightly antiaromatic regions, highlighting the intrinsic electronic frustration associated with the nonalternant topology. These findings demonstrate how the controlled incorporation of [7–5–5] motifs enables the rational bandgap engineering in carbon-based polymers and expands the scope of nonbenzenoid design in on-surface synthesis.

missingCandidates.title: Reactivity and Selectivity of Photocatalytic Nitrate Reduction Reaction to Ammonia: Pt, Pd, Ir, and Rh Single Atoms on p-Type TiO2 Nanotubes
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract We present a systematic study of noble metal (Pt, Pd, Ir, and Rh) single-atom cocatalysts decorated on p-type and quantum-confined TiO2 nanotubes for photocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia. All single-atom cocatalysts were prepared through a reactive deposition using different metal precursors, resulting in a single-atom oxidation state (δ+) of δ ≈ 2. At a similar loading concentration (0.2–0.3 at%) and in the absence of any sacrificial agent, Pd single atoms exhibit the highest element-specific activity for ammonia production, while Pt single atoms display a prominent photocatalytic activity with a strong tendency of nitrite reduction toward ammonia. Rh single atoms achieve the highest ammonia selectivity, whereas Ir single atoms predominantly produce nitrite due to inhibited subsequent reduction. Comparisons with single atoms deposited on conventional TiO2 (P25) and with nanoparticles supported on the nanotubes reveal that both the semiconductor properties (quantum confinement effect and p-type conductivity) and the speciation of the cocatalyst (single atom) can significantly enhance activity and selectivity. These findings aid in establishing design principles for different single-atom catalysts toward efficient and selective photocatalytic nitrogen valorization.

missingCandidates.title: Redox Properties of the Copper Centers in Particulate Methane Monooxygenase
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Particulate methane monooxygenase (pMMO) and its homolog ammonia monooxygenase (AMO), central enzymes in the global carbon and nitrogen cycles, contain three highly conserved mononuclear copper centers, denoted CuB, CuC, and CuD. While these sites have been well characterized structurally and spectroscopically, with recent studies identifying CuD as the active site, their reduction potentials have not been measured. This knowledge gap has hindered efforts to determine how the two electrons and two protons required for substrate oxidation are sourced and delivered. Here, we have elucidated the redox properties of each copper center in pMMO/AMO by protein film voltammetry using samples with copper occupancies known from cryoelectron microscopy (cryoEM) structures. The reduction potential of the CuB site, −72 to −139 mV, is significantly lower than the ∼400 mV measured for the CuD site, with consistent values determined for pMMOs and AMO from different species. Mutation of a residue in the second sphere of CuB, Glu35, alters the redox potential and impairs cell growth and pMMO activity, indicating that redox chemistry at CuB might be functionally relevant. Finally, a Pourbaix diagram constructed for the CuBII/I and CuDII/I half-reactions suggests that a proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) process occurs at the CuD site but not at the CuB site. Thermochemical analysis of this proposed PCET process is compatible with electron delivery by a quinol reductant. These results provide new context for future investigations of the pMMO and AMO reaction mechanisms.

missingCandidates.title: Redox-Induced Polymeric Micelle-to-Coacervate Transition for Enhanced Endosomal Escape, Prolonged Drug Retention, and Improved Sequential Drug Delivery
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Polymeric micelles (PMs) and coacervate microdroplets (CMs) are both promising delivery vehicles, yet each suffers from distinct limitations. The delivery efficiency of PMs is often hindered by factors, such as limited endosome escape and uncontrolled drug release. On the other hand, CMs are prone to coalescence and aging, which hamper long-term storage and systemic injection. Here, by employing an intracellular morphological transition strategy, these drawbacks can be efficiently addressed without compromising their inherent advantages. The system exists as nanosized PMs during storage and circulation. Upon internalization by the tumor cells, the highly reductive intracellular environment induces the detachment of the poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) shell and results in in situ formation of CMs. The formed CMs can effectively escape from endosomes by disrupting the endosomal membrane, facilitating the release of drugs into the cytoplasm. Furthermore, the CMs can serve as drug reservoirs, protecting the cargo from burst release and degradation, thus significantly prolonging the retention time and improving systemic delivery efficacy. Notably, the CMs can also sequester free drugs from the surrounding environment, enhancing sequential therapy by increasing the intratumoral accumulation of the temporally staggered agents. Thus, this micelle-to-coacervate transformable platform illuminates new possibilities for both types of drug-delivery systems.

missingCandidates.title: Tailoring Superhydrophobic Ultramicropores in Covalent Organic Frameworks for Humidity-Resistant Methane Purification
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Efficient purification of methane from raw natural gas under humid conditions remains challenging because water adsorption often degrades the separation performance and structural stability of porous adsorbents. Here we report a topology- and stacking-guided molecular design strategy that integrates ultramicropore engineering with pore-surface fluorination to construct superhydrophobic covalent organic frameworks (COFs) for humidity-resistant methane purification. Two isoreticular fluorinated COFs, TF-COF and NF-COF, were constructed by rationally controlling framework topology and interlayer stacking, generating well-defined ultramicropores for size-selective discrimination of C1–C3 hydrocarbons. Fluorination simultaneously enhances pore-wall hydrophobicity and strengthens host–guest interactions, creating a confined adsorption environment that promotes hydrocarbon recognition while effectively suppressing competitive water adsorption. As a result, NF-COF exhibits a propane uptake of 99.4 cm3 g–1 and an exceptional C3H8/CH4 IAST selectivity of 251.7 at 298 K. Dynamic breakthrough experiments further demonstrate efficient methane purification under both dry and highly humid conditions, with the separation performance fully retained at 97% relative humidity owing to its superhydrophobic surface. Theoretical calculations reveal that densely distributed fluorine atoms generate synergistic pore confinement and multiple C–H···F van der Waals interactions, simultaneously maximizing adsorption capacity and molecular discrimination. These findings establish fluorinated superhydrophobic COFs as a robust platform for energy-efficient natural gas upgrading under industrially relevant humid conditions.

missingCandidates.title: The Molecular Logic of Platelet-Activating Factor (PAF)
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Platelet-activating factor (PAF) is a well-known if enigmatic lipid signal with important roles in inflammatory responses, allergic reactions, autoimmune diseases, and thrombotic cascades. Several lines of evidence suggest that our current model of PAF’s molecular mechanism is inadequate. This report describes a recontextualized model for PAF. The revised model embeds PAF in a plasmalogen-based molecular mechanism in which activation is a spontaneous chemical reaction triggered by environmental conditions that liberates a PAF receptor (PAF-R) agonist from a membrane-bound phospholipid. The active ligand subsequently undergoes a thermodynamically driven spontaneous rearrangement into an inactive isomer, a feature that controls response lifetime. The revised model is a molecule-autonomous set of transformations that create a response with spatial and temporal control. More generally the revised model’s congruence with a similar model for RORγt supports a picture in which plasmalogens form a part of the immune system that is separate from the cell-based innate and adaptive immune systems.

missingCandidates.title: Unlocking the Tertiary Nitrogen Effect in 3D Anisotropic Covalent Organic Frameworks to Achieve Record Iodine Capture under Industrial Conditions
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Using porous adsorbents to achieve efficient capture of radioactive iodine from nuclear waste under industrial conditions remains a formidable challenge, since most adsorbents just exhibit a low iodine uptake under such conditions. We herein show two 3D [8 + 4]-assembled covalent organic frameworks (COFs, ECUT-COF-99 and ECUT-COF-100) for this challenging target. The two COFs feature a minimal-transitivity [3 4] flu-derived net, which allows anisotropic isoreticular expansion through a general sequential derived-net approach. ECUT-COF-100 was found to give an ultrahigh iodine uptake of 1.51 g/g under simulated industrial conditions (150 °C and 150 ppmv I2), 5.2-fold that of ECUT-COF-99 (0.29 g/g). Such performance also far exceeds all established organic adsorbents for this use. Mechanism studies reveal that nonaromatic tertiary nitrogen atoms allow for strong charge transfer from the lone-pair electrons of tertiary nitrogen to I2, leading to the formation of ionic iodides (I3– and I5–) and the N·+ radical cation and then fixing of ionic iodides by Coulomb interactions. This work not only provides a promising adsorbent with record iodine uptake for radioactive iodine capture from nuclear waste but also highlights a new insight into the tertiary nitrogen effect in 3D COFs for efficient iodine capture.

Although current treatments may alleviate some of these symptoms, the intricate pathogenesis of these comorbidities highlights an urgent need for therapeutic strategies with combined anti-inflammatory, barrier-reparative, and microbiota-modulating effects. Herein, we develop a series of nanozyme-exoskeletonized yeast-derived polysaccharides (NZEP) by integrating nanozymes with yeast-derived polysaccharides using an insect sclerotization-inspired strategy. Among them, NZEP TA-Ce , with the highest degree of nanozyme-exoskeletonization, is capable of disrupting the inflammatory vicious cycle by inhibiting MAPK and NF-κB-mediated inflammatory signaling pathways. Furthermore, NZEP TA-Ce treatment reverses gut microbiota dysbiosis and optimizes the composition of microbial metabolites, thereby alleviating anxiety and depressive symptoms associated with IBD. This study provides a safe and promising therapeutic strategy for the management of IBD patients and their associated psychological comorbidities.

missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Clay minerals are the most crucial constituents in brickmaking clays, yet the specific role of different clay minerals remain poorly understood due to their natural coexistence and formidable challenges of separation. Here, we design a kaolinite-illite-quartz-feldspar system through a multiple-stage purification strategy, enabling direct evaluation of two of the most critical clay minerals for brick making - kaolinite and illite. missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis (ICI-myocarditis) is a rare but frequently fatal immune-related adverse event. A comprehensive understanding of the cellular and molecular determinants driving ICI-myocarditis is essential for improving diagnostic precision and developing targeted interventions. We delineate the immune landscape of ICI-myocarditis via scRNA-seq, flow cytometry, Olink proteomics, and multiplex cytokine profiling. We demonstrate that high levels of baseline ISG15⁺CD8⁺ T cells are linked to the proinflammatory features of monocytes and in vitro experiments confirm the existence of circulating ISG15⁺CD8⁺ T cells with a high potential to induce cardiomyocyte apoptosis, supporting their pathogenic potential for cardiomyocyte cytotoxicity. In summary, this study implicates immune-pathogenic features of ICI-myocarditis and provides a possible basis for future therapies.

missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Anti-tuberculosis (TB) drugs must reach the disease site to be effective, but complex TB pathology limits drug distribution and efficacy, as bacteria in the necrotic center of lung cavities are difficult to access and kill. We validate a lung lesion penetration model with clinical data and develop an integrated approach that combines microenvironment-specific pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Next, we simulate site-of-disease coverage of shortened regimens tested in major Phase 3 trials over the past decade, allowing direct comparisons with trial outcomes. We propose that regimens including at least two drugs achieving bactericidal concentrations in pulmonary cavities are more likely to meet primary clinical endpoints in patients with cavitary disease. Our translational platform constitutes a validated tool to support drug evaluation, smart regimen design, and de-risking of late-stage trials.

Along-strike variations in coseismic and interseismic deformation reveal a helix-shaped fault geometry. The average coseismic slip equals or exceeds the interseismic slip deficit, consistent with a minimally slip-predictable model. We generate an ensemble of 3D dynamic rupture models, constrained by the best-fit static slip model, then discriminate among them using independent space-geodetic, seismic, and near-field video observations. These dynamics are shaped by localized stress heterogeneity and low fracture energy, characteristic of a structurally mature fault zone. Our approach can inform rupture scenarios in understudied regions.

missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Quantifying three-dimensional (3D) orientation is critical for understanding self-assembly and collective behavior in soft matter and biological systems. Moreover, orientational analysis of anisotropic particles can characterize locally applied forces in fluids. We develop a confocal imaging setup optimized for lanthanide luminescence and a theoretical framework to extract both the local director and order parameter in nanorod assemblies. The technique achieves 0.5 μm lateral and 1 μm axial spatial resolution and is demonstrated in dense nematic liquid-crystal assemblies, resolving complex 3D topological structures, and in microfluidic flows, mapping alignment under hydrodynamic shear. This approach provides a versatile platform for quantitative studies of collective orientation, self-assembly mechanics, and alignment induced by external forces, and can be extended to other lanthanide-labeled particles and molecular probes.

missingCandidates.title: Regulation of PDH via cysteine oxidation on DLAT
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex is a key regulator of metabolism, controlling flux from glycolysis into the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. PDH is often dysregulated in metabolic diseases and cancer. We discover here that in addition to its well characterized regulation by phosphorylation, PDH activity is also regulated via inhibitory oxidation of three cysteines of the DLAT subunit - Cys488, Cys586 and Cys618. Oxidation of these cysteines increases under oxidative stress, and is highly prevalent in mouse and human tissues. This mechanism enables cells to efficiently fight oxidative stress. Under oxidative stress, cells execute a metabolic shift, blocking glycolytic flux into the TCA cycle to shunt glycolytic carbons toward the pentose phosphate pathway. This generates NADPH which cells use to detoxify H 2 O 2 and to reduce oxidized cysteines. We find that DLAT oxidation is required for cells to mount an effective antioxidant response. Mutations preventing DLAT oxidation render PDH resistant to oxidative inhibition, impair NADPH generation, reduce peroxide detoxification, and sensitize cells to oxidative damage and death. DLAT oxidation also drives a Warburg-like metabolic phenotype of increased glucose uptake, elevated lactate secretion, and reduced TCA cycle activity. Thus DLAT oxidation is a redox-sensing mechanism that regulates PDH activity and central carbon metabolism.

Using biophysical and genomic arguments, we introduce an evolutionary model of HK97-fold protein shells, predicting that they emerged as lower-symmetry biochemical compartments and that HK97-fold viral capsids may retain biochemical functions.

Vacancy-mediated ultrafast oxide-ion conduction in excess-oxygen Sillén oxybromides
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) require electrolytes with high oxide-ion conductivity at low temperatures (200–400 °C) to reduce costs. Here, we report that Bi 1.9 Te 0.1 LaO 4.05 Br exhibits oxide-ion conductivity of 0.01 S cm⁻¹ at 233 °C within the “Norby gap” in dry atmospheres. This performance exceeds that of leading proton conductors, such as BaZr 0.8 Y 0.2 O 2.9 and BaZr 0.4 Ce 0.4 Y 0.1 Yb 0.1 O 2.9 , as well as representative oxide-ion conductors, including yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ), LaGaO 3 -based phases (LSGM), and Bi 2 V 0.7 Sb 0.3 O 5.5 . Bi 1.9 Te 0.1 LaO 4.05 Br also exhibits negligible chemical expansion and high chemical stability under oxidizing, reducing, and CO 2 -containing atmospheres. The high conductivity is associated with a layered Sillén structure composed of Bi-containing triple fluorite-like slabs and Br layers, together with oxygen vacancies that enable vacancy-mediated oxide-ion migration. Despite the presence of excess oxide ions, oxide-ion transport predominantly occurs via a vacancy mechanism, as revealed by ab initio molecular dynamics simulations, static density functional theory calculations, and neutron diffraction analyses. These findings establish a design principle for high-performance oxide-ion conductors based on vacancy-mediated oxide-ion transport in excess-oxygen Bi-containing Sillén oxyhalides.

Bicyclic BODIPY-Submonoazaporphyrin Hybrids via a Catalyst-Free SNAr Strategy: Coexisting Local Aromaticity and Global Antiaromaticity with Broad NIR-II Absorption
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract A series of bicyclic BODIPY-submonoazaporphyrin hybrids were efficiently constructed via a catalyst-free SNAr strategy, exhibiting excellent chemical stability. These hybrids exhibit a unique coexistence of local 14π aromaticity and global 28π antiaromaticity, which was unambiguously verified by NMR spectroscopy and theoretical calculations. Moreover, they show remarkably broad UV–vis–NIR absorption spanning the range of 300–1400 nm (NIR-II) and rich redox properties, thereby providing an effective strategy for designing novel porphyrinoids with tunable aromaticity as stable NIR functional materials.

missingCandidates.title: Controlled Generation of Unstabilized N -Alkyl Nitrile Imines Enables Regioselective (3 + 2) Cycloadditions with Diverse Dipolarophiles
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract N-Alkyl nitrile imines remain underdeveloped as intermediates for intermolecular cycloadditions. Here, we report their in situ generation and regioselective (3 + 2) cycloaddition with activated and unactivated alkenes and alkynes, affording N-alkyl pyrazolines and pyrazoles in good to excellent yields. The method accommodates broad variation in both reaction partners and enables gram-scale preparation of a key pyrazole fragment used in the synthesis of lenacapavir in a 79% yield over two steps.

missingCandidates.title: Criegee Intermediate-Enabled Decarboxylative C(sp3)–C(sp3) Cross-Coupling of α,β-Unsaturated Esters with Cyclic Acetals
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Ozonolysis and Baeyer–Villiger (BV) rearrangement are among the earliest transformations in which cyclic/acyclic peroxo intermediates, often known as Criegee intermediates, have been detected. Herein, we disclose the merger of a Criegee intermediate with C(sp3)–C(sp3) cross-coupling via a rare anti-Giese addition for a new genre of C–C cross-coupling to access complex chemical libraries. Detailed mechanistic investigation reveals the generation of a cyclic tetrahedral peroxo intermediate (CI), and gas-phase analysis establishes the formation of 16O═C═18O under 18O2 conditions and straightforwardly supports the formation of peroxylactones via a Criegee intermediate under our standard conditions. Importantly, many pharmaceutically active drug-like molecules have been screened thoroughly and have been shown to exhibit excellent tolerance and high regioselectivity for this methodology.

missingCandidates.title: Dihydrogen Phosphate Anion-Templated Synthesis of Urethane-Based Macrocycle Containing Perfluoroalkyl Chain
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract The efficient synthesis of macrocycles has been a challenging subject in supramolecular chemistry. This study shows that H2PO4– acts as a template in the synthesis of novel macrocycles containing a long perfluoroalkyl chain in their backbone. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations indicate that H2PO4– preorganizes the reaction intermediate in the transition state through multiple hydrogen-bonding interactions, promoting the cyclization reaction and increasing the yield of the macrocycle. The introduction of the fluoroalkyl chain increases the acidity of the neighboring CH2 group, thereby enhancing the hydrogen-bonding interactions in the intermediate complex.

missingCandidates.title: Multidimensional Involvement of Tris(4-methoxyphenyl)amine in Electrolytic Sulfonylation of Alkenes
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract A tris(4-methoxyphenyl)amine (TMPA)-catalyzed paired-electrolysis sulfonylation is reported. TMPA first serves as the electron donor, thereby facilitating the reduction of sulfonyl chloride; subsequently, the resulting TMPA•+ oxidizes the benzyl radical intermediate. TMPA and the chloride anion also act as a Brønsted base to promote deprotonation at the α-carbon of the sulfonyl group. The current results elucidate a novel paradigm of triarylamine multiple activation, which may stimulate continuous exploration of multiple action modes of other mediators.

missingCandidates.title: Pd-Catalyzed Freon-Enabled Aminocarbonylation of Aryl Iodides
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract A palladium-catalyzed Freon-to-carbonyl transfer strategy has been developed for the CO-free aminocarbonylation of aryl and heteroaryl iodides with amines. Using chlorodifluoromethane (Freon-22) as both a difluorocarbene precursor and a carbonyl source, this protocol enables direct access to diverse benzamide derivatives without external CO gas or conventional CO-releasing reagents. The reaction exhibits a broad substrate scope and good functional-group tolerance, accommodating electronically diverse aryl iodides, polycyclic and heteroaryl iodides, and primary and secondary amines. Its synthetic utility is demonstrated by late-stage benzamidation of bioactive-molecule-derived substrates and concise synthesis of pharmaceutically relevant benzamide scaffolds, including trimethobenzamide and methyl tamibarotene. Mechanistic experiments involving benzimidazole trapping and H218O labeling support a difluorocarbene-derived carbonyl-transfer process in which water contributes to the oxygen atom of the amide carbonyl group. This work establishes Freon-22 as a practical carbonyl surrogate for CO-free amide synthesis.

missingCandidates.title: Photocatalytic Scaffold Hopping of Cyclobutanols to Cyclopentanols via Single-Carbon Insertion into C–C σ-Bonds
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract A method for skeletal editing of C–C σ-bonds in strained alicycles via single-carbon insertion is reported. This skeletal editing method for cyclobutanols differs from well-established semipinacol rearrangement pathways, offering an efficient route to cyclopentanols by direct scaffold hopping of cyclobutanols. This transformation proceeds under mild conditions in good yields, expanding the toolkit for single-atom insertion into C–C σ-bonds.

missingCandidates.title: Planar Bis(1,3,4-Oxadiazole) Bridging toward High-Energy and Low-Sensitivity Tetracyclic Compounds
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract A planar bis(1,3,4-oxadiazole) bridging strategy was developed to access rigid, extended-conjugated tetracyclic energetic compounds. Incorporation of this bridge into two distinct energetic scaffolds afforded 4 and 7. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction revealed a nearly planar bis(1,3,4-oxadiazole) bridge in both compounds, accompanied by extended π-electron delocalization across the molecular frameworks. Compound 4 showed enhanced thermal and mechanical stability, while 7 combined improved energetic performance with increased stability.

missingCandidates.title: Scaffold Hopping of Pyrimidines into 2-Acylpyrroles
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract A practical skeletal-editing strategy was developed for the conversion of 4-substituted pyrimidines into 2-acyl-5-arylpyrroles. The transformation directly converts a six-membered, electron-deficient pyrimidine into a five-membered azole while simultaneously installing an acyl group. The reaction sequence involves pyrimidine activation, ring-opening, fragmentation, and ring reconstruction. Central to this strategy is the controlled generation of pyrimidine-derived vinamidinium salts as open-chain A4 synthons, which are then intercepted by α-bromoketones as functionalized annulation reagents. The developed scaffold-hopping method can be applied for late-stage modification of pyrimidine-containing bioactive or pharmaceutical molecules.

missingCandidates.title: Solid-Phase Synthesis of Enteropeptin A Analogues
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract Enteropeptin A is a sactipeptide natural product featuring a unique six-membered thiomorpholine core. Herein, we describe a solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS)-compatible approach to enteropeptin A analogues featuring a simplified sactionine motif. The strategy employs a readily accessible building block and efficient on-resin assembly. A “N to C” variant, differing in the directionality of the sactionine linkage was also readily accessible. Collectively, this work accelerates access to analogues of this important class of natural products.

missingCandidates.title: Stereoselective Synthesis of Linustedastat Via Deoxy-Aromatization Strategy
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract An efficient and stereoselective synthesis of Linustedastat (1) is reported, commencing from inexpensive and commercially available sitolactone. The route features a highly chemoselective Grignard addition, followed by sequential double aldol condensations to construct the core steroidal framework. A key step involves a novel deoxy-aromatization of a fluorinated steroid intermediate, setting the stage for a stereoselective hydrogenation and a 1,4-conjugate addition to further elaborate the molecule. This strategically designed sequence delivers the complex and electron-deficient fluorinated steroidal architecture in 16 steps with an 11.0% overall yield.

missingCandidates.title: Synthesis of α-Cyano-β-naphthylamines via Tandem Selective Hydrocyanation of Unactivated Alkynes and Thorpe Reaction
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract An unprecedented nickel-catalyzed tandem reaction involving alkyne hydrocyanation and sequential Thorpe reaction has been developed. By employing readily available and less toxic Zn(CN)2 as the cyanide source, both selective alkyne hydrocyanation and tandem cyclization are achieved in a substrate-controlled manner. Mechanistic studies and DFT calculations confirm that the alkenyl nitrile serves as a key intermediate, and hydrogen transfer is identified as the rate-determining step in the Thorpe reaction. This work offers a novel strategy for the construction of α-cyano-β-naphthylamine via a cascade reaction mode.

missingCandidates.title: Divergent Kinetics and Rate-Determining Steps for 1-Butene and 2-Butene Hydroformylation with a Bidentate Phosphoramidite Ligand: A Combined Experimental and Density Functional Theory Study
missingCandidates.abstract: Abstract The hydroformylation of mixed butenes (1-butene and 2-butene) to n-valeraldehyde is an important industrial process, yet the distinct kinetic behaviors of the two isomers under identical catalytic conditions remain insufficiently understood. Herein, a comprehensive kinetic and mechanistic investigation of 1-butene and 2-butene was conducted using a robust, water- and air-stable, highly regioselective bidentate phosphoramidite ligand-modified rhodium catalyst in a homogeneous system. Systematic kinetic experiments revealed that the hydroformylation of 2-butene exhibits a strong positive dependence on H2 pressure and obvious substrate inhibition at high concentrations, whereas 1-butene shows little H2 dependence and no substrate inhibition. Using a semi-empirical hyperbolic kinetic modeling, the rate equations capture these distinct behaviors with high accuracy (R2 = 0.9746 for 2-butene, 0.9642 for 1-butene). Kinetic studies revealed distinct rate behaviors for 1-butene and 2-butene hydroformylation. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations on the n-valeraldehyde pathway further showed that hydride insertion to the internal C═C double bond has the highest barrier for 2-butene, while CO insertion to the linear rhodium n-butyl intermediate has the highest barrier for 1-butene, providing the mechanistic origin for the observed kinetic differences. The iso-valeraldehyde pathway is additionally disfavored by a 2.7 kcal·mol–1 higher RDS barrier, consistent with the good n-selectivity. In situ high-pressure FTIR spectroscopy further confirmed the five-coordinate hydride HRh(CO)2(P)2 as the catalyst resting state. These findings offer quantitative guidance for optimizing industrial hydroformylation processes using mixed butene feedstocks.

missingCandidates.title: Architecting 3D Space‐Charge Heterointerfacial Networks for Electrode‐Scale Ion Transport
missingCandidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Harnessing space‐charge effects to govern carrier dynamics is central to nanoionics, yet translating localized nanoscale transport into continuous electrode‐wide percolation remains challenging. Here, we report an architectural strategy that uses Na 2 O/Na 2 CO 3 heterointerfaces as local nanoionic transport units and organizes them into a bulk‐distributed, three‐dimensional network throughout a preformed electrode. This architecture is realized by coupling ultralow‐flux Na‐vapor metallization with mesopore‐regulated gas‐solid conversion in a preformed metal‐organic framework (MOF) host. The synergy of space‐charge carrier enrichment and MOF‐mediated lattice distortion simultaneously boosts carrier density and lowers migration barriers, yielding an estimated local interfacial conductivity on the order of 10 −7 S cm −1 at 25°C, from intrinsically insulating Na 2 O (10 −12 S cm −1 ) and Na 2 CO 3 (10 −23 S cm −1 ). Integrated with conducting carbon, this functionally percolating network enables stable solid‐state presodiation and ultrahigh‐rate sodium‐ion full cells. This work bridges the gap between nanoscopic interface physics and macroscopic device functionality, identifying the spatial connectivity of phase boundaries, rather than the localized space‐charge effect alone, as a programmable design variable for next‐generation solid‐state ionics.

missingCandidates.title: Generation and Stabilization of Soliton‐Type Radicals in Amidine‐Linked Porous Oligoacetylene Polymers by Topological Confinement Strategy for Photothermal Catalysis
missingCandidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Porous polymers incorporating stable organic radicals are typically limited to a handful of known radical types. Here, we introduce a topological confinement strategy that generates a previously inaccessible class of open‑shell species: neutral soliton‑type radicals, within amidine‑linked oligoacetylene networks. In chemical terms, these species are characterized by a delocalized spin density over the conjugated backbone, distinguishing them from conventional localized radicals. These materials exhibit a distinct axial g ‑tensor, Curie behavior, and broad near‑infrared absorption extending to 1000 nm. Unlike conventional photothermal systems, where heat originates from exciton transfer energy to the lattice via nonradiative processes, our system stores light energy in long‐lived soliton states that dissipate via lattice vibrations, producing no ground‑state bleach yet enabling efficient heat generation. Using this mechanism, the materials drive aldehyde‑indole coupling under mild light irradiation through a photothermal catalytic pathway. More broadly, this work translates soliton physics into a synthetic materials platform for spin‑functional materials.

missingCandidates.title: Hierarchically Molecular Programming of Antiparallel H‑Aggregates for NIR Type I Photochemistry
missingCandidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Developing near‐infrared (NIR) photosensitizers with effective type I reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation remains challenging. H‑aggregates promote triplet formation and charge transfer, but often suffer from substantial absorption blueshifts and excessive thermal deactivation that compromise photosensitization efficacy. Herein, a hierarchically molecular programming strategy is proposed to construct minimal‐blueshift H‐aggregates as robust NIR type I photosensitizers. Primary engineering via π‐bridge extension and acceptor strengthening within a twisted–planar donor–π–acceptor scaffold endows the antiparallel H‐packed TNCF3‐C6‐C2 aggregates with strong NIR absorption (749 nm) and predominant type I ROS generation. Secondary side‐chain programming further regulates the H‐packing and intermolecular electronic interactions to enhance type I ROS generation. Structural, photochemical and theoretical investigations revealed that the branched side chains promote molecular planarization and robust H‑packing, thereby enhancing intersystem crossing and intermolecular charge transfer. The optimized TNCF3‐2C6 with symmetric branched side chain exhibited minimal absorption blueshift (20 nm) upon H‐aggregation, enhanced NIR harvesting ability and a further ∼2‐fold enhancement in ROS generation over the initial TNCF3‐C6‐C2 H‐aggregates, thereby delivering potent tumor inhibition both in vitro and in vivo. Built upon the hierarchical programming of H‐aggregates, this work establishes a supramolecular design paradigm toward modulating excitonic coupling and excited‐state dynamics for high‐performance photo‐functional materials.

missingCandidates.title: Perturbation of the Electron Transport Chain by Guanidinium‐Based Cationic Polymers Induces Metabolic Collapse in Persister‐Enriched Bacterial Populations
missingCandidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Bacterial persisters are widely regarded as dormant or hypometabolic cells that survive antibiotic treatment with suppressed metabolic activity. Here, we show that this apparent quiescence is accompanied by a heightened vulnerability to electron transport chain (ETC)‐associated perturbation by guanidinium‐based cationic polymers. PO 3 G, a representative polymer, preferentially kills persister‐enriched populations while markedly perturbing respiratory electron transfer. Following this ETC‐associated perturbation, persister‐enriched populations exhibit sustained superoxide‐associated oxidative stress and fail to restore NADH/NAD + homeostasis, leading to progressive loss of viability. Consistent with this ETC dependency, PO 3 G also markedly reduces persister‐enriched population induced by diverse triggers across bacterial species and achieves up to 7‐log reductions in bacterial burden in vivo. These results establish a mechanistic link between cationic polymer‐induced ETC‐associated perturbation and persister elimination, highlighting limited recovery from respiratory and redox perturbation as a vulnerability underlying the preferential killing of persisters.

Control experiments and density functional theory (DFT) calculations support an SNAr/cyclization mechanism. Preliminary photophysical studies show that the products exhibit blue emission, suggesting potential applications in materials science. Additionally, molecular docking studies indicate that the synthesized scaffold may have relevance to medicinal chemistry, providing a foundation for future biological evaluations.
